sections.title: Section A: The British sector of the Western Front, 1914–18: injuries, treatment and the trenches

topics.title: 1. The Context of the British Sector of the Western Front

points.point_text: **The Historical Context of Medicine in the Early Twentieth Century:** The understanding of infection & moves towards aseptic surgery (autoclaves, rubber gloves, surgical gowns); the development of X-rays (Wilhelm Roentgen 1895, early diagnostic use, radiation hazards); blood transfusions & developments in the storage of blood (James Blundell 1818, Karl Landsteiner blood groups A, B, O in 1901 & AB in 1902, problem of coagulation preventing pre-war storage)

points.point_text: **The Theatre of War in Flanders & Northern France:** The context of the British sector of the Western Front: the vulnerable Ypres salient (surrounded by higher German ridges; First Ypres 1914, Second Ypres 1915 with first poison gas, Third Ypres/Passchendaele 1917 with waterlogged liquid mud; mining at Hill 60), the Somme (July 1916, 57,000 day 1 casualties), Arras (April 1917, chalk quarries & 2.5 miles of tunnels) & Cambrai (November 1917, mass tank deployment)

points.point_text: **The Trench System — Organisation & Construction:** Frontline firing trenches (firestep, sandbag parapet, parados), support trenches (80m behind), reserve trenches (100m+ behind) & communication trenches linking them for safe movement of troops, supplies & wounded; Zigzag traverse design to localise artillery shell blasts & prevent enfilade rifle fire
points.teacher_note: ⚠️ UNEXAMINED TOPIC: Not assessed in the 2018–2025 public exam series. Prime territory for upcoming classroom mocks and revision.

points.point_text: **Terrain, Transport & Communications Infrastructure:** The catastrophic impact of waterlogged clay, destroyed natural drainage & massive artillery cratering; Problems for medical evacuation: heavy motor ambulances getting bogged down, reliance on 6-horse ambulance wagons & stretcher-bearers navigating liquid mud under fire; Communication problems: artillery severing telephone cables, forcing medical staff to rely on runner messengers, carrier pigeons & visual flags under fire

points.point_text: **Ill Health Arising from the Trench Environment:** Trench foot (cold waterlogged mud, restricted circulation, gangrene; treated with whale oil, dry socks, pair inspections, amputation); Trench fever (pyrexia, body lice in clothing seams, flu-like aches; treated with delousing stations, affected 500,000 men); Shell shock / NYD.N ('Not Yet Diagnosed, Nervous' — severe psychological trauma, tremors, mental collapse; 80,000 casualties treated at Craiglockhart Hospital, Edinburgh)

points.point_text: **The Nature of Wounds from Modern Weaponry:** High-explosive artillery shells & shrapnel (jagged metal fragments, causing 58% of all wounds & massive trauma); machine guns & rifles (causing 39% of wounds, shattering bones & piercing organs)

points.point_text: **The Problem of Wound Infection:** Deeply fertilised agricultural soil packed with anaerobic manure bacteria causing lethal tetanus & gas gangrene (rapid tissue necrosis & gas bubbles; anti-tetanus serum introduced late 1914; failure of peacetime antiseptics)

points.point_text: **The Effects of Poison Gas Attacks:** Chlorine gas (Second Ypres, April 1915, suffocation & pulmonary edema; urine pads used before gas masks); Phosgene gas (December 1915, faster-acting & highly lethal); Mustard gas (1917, odourless blister agent burning skin through clothing & causing temporary blindness); Overall gas mortality kept under 5% by rapid introduction of box respirators

points.point_text: **The Stages of the Chain of Evacuation:** (1) Regimental Aid Post (RAP, within 200m of frontline, first aid from Regimental Medical Officer); (2) Field Ambulance & Dressing Stations (ADS/MDS, 400m to half a mile back, temporary triage & emergency treatment); (3) Casualty Clearing Station (CCS, 7–12 miles back near railheads, priority triage into walking wounded, hospital cases & moribund; performed urgent forward surgery for gas gangrene & compound fractures); (4) Base Hospitals (coastal ports at Calais, Boulogne, Le Havre; specialist wards for head wounds, burns & gas; evacuation to 'Blighty')

sections.title: Section B: Medicine in Britain, c1250–present

topics.title: Unit 1: Medicine in Medieval England, c1250–c1500

points.point_text: **Ideas about the Cause of Disease & Illness:** Supernatural & religious explanations: disease as divine retribution from God for sin, test of faith, or demonic influence; astrology & planetary alignments (e.g. 1345 alignment of Mars, Jupiter & Saturn blamed for Black Death); Rational explanations: Hippocrates' Theory of the Four Humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile; illness caused by internal imbalance); the Miasma theory (bad air & poisonous vapours corrupted by rotting matter); continuing authority of Galen (Theory of Opposites; Church control of universities & monasteries enforcing Galenic dogma; ban on human dissection)

points.point_text: **Approaches to Prevention & Treatment:** Treatments linked to beliefs: religious actions (prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, flagellation, touching relics); humoural treatments: bloodletting (phlebotomy via venesection, cupping & leeches) & purging (emetics, laxatives, clysters); purifying the air (pomanders, sweet herbs, street fires); traditional herbal remedies (Theriaca, Materia Medica); Traditional practitioners: university-trained physicians (7–10 years study, urine charts, astrology, expensive, 'care not cure'); apothecaries (herbal mixtures, accessible to ordinary people); barber surgeons (apprenticeship, tooth-pulling, bloodletting, basic amputations); Role of hospitals (c1,100 by 1500, run by Church monks & nuns, hospitality & rest, infectious/terminal patients rejected); care in the community & home by women

topics.title: Unit 3: Medicine in 18th- and 19th-Century Britain, c1700–c1900

points.point_text: **Ideas about the Cause of Disease & Illness:** Continuity in early period: spontaneous generation (microbes appear spontaneously in decaying matter) & miasma; Louis Pasteur's Germ Theory (1861, swan-neck flask experiments proved airborne microbes cause decay & fermentation; 1878 germ theory of disease); reception in Britain: initial resistance from Dr Charlton Bastian & traditionalists, gradual acceptance through John Tyndall (1870s) & Joseph Lister; Robert Koch's work on microbes: 'microbe hunting', agar jelly culture plates, industrial chemical dyes to photograph bacteria; isolated specific disease pathogens: anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) & cholera (1883)

points.point_text: **Approaches to Prevention, Treatment & Hospital Care:** Improvements in hospitals: Florence Nightingale (Crimean War 1854, Notes on Nursing 1859, pavilion hospital design, sanitation, ventilation, professional nurse training school at St Thomas's; mortality dropped from 40% to 2%); Development of anaesthetics: laughing gas (1844), ether (1846), James Simpson & chloroform (1847); opposition to anaesthetics (pain seen as God's will, danger of overdose); Queen Victoria's use of chloroform in childbirth (1853); surgical 'Black Period' as deeper operations caused infection; Development of antiseptics: Joseph Lister & carbolic acid spray (1865/1867, inspired by Pasteur, cut surgical mortality from 46% to 15%); transition by 1890s to aseptic surgery (autoclaves, rubber gloves, sterile gowns); Public Health reform: Edwin Chadwick's report (1842), Public Health Act 1848 (permissive); Great Stink (1858) & Joseph Bazalgette's London sewer network; Public Health Act 1875 (compulsory provision of clean water, sewers, street lighting, food inspection, medical officers)
